name: Martin of Tours

seo.title: St Martin of Tours: the cloak, his miracles and his feast days
seo.description: Who Martin of Tours was, in plain words: the cloak, his miracles, his feast days East and West, and his words with the book and chapter.

band.lede: Soldier turned monk and bishop, and one of the best loved saints of Gaul.

picture.alt: Saint Martin on a white horse cuts his green cloak with his sword for a beggar, by El Greco
picture.credit: Saint Martin and the Beggar, El Greco, 1597-1599. National Gallery of Art, Washington. CC0.
picture.creator: El Greco

card.line: Soldier turned monk and bishop, and one of the best loved saints of Gaul.

who: Martin was a Roman cavalryman who became a monk, then bishop of Tours in Gaul. He is best known for cutting his cloak in two for a freezing beggar. He founded what may be the first monastery in Gaul. He refused to flatter an emperor. He was one of the first saints honoured who did not die a martyr.

About 61, if he was born in 336

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 316. Some scholars say about 336. At Savaria in Pannonia, today **Szombathely in Hungary**.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At Ticinum, today **Pavia in Italy**. His parents were pagans.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **8 November 397**, at Candes in his own diocese. He had a fever, and he was old.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Martin the Merciful**, in the Russian Church and the OCA. **Martin the Wonderworker**, in Greek.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Cutting his cloak in two with his sword for a beggar, usually on horseback.

facts.label: Pronounced
facts.text: **MAR-tin of TOOR**. The s in Tours is silent.

portrait.alt: An icon on gold: the young Martin on a grey horse cuts his red cloak with a sword for a beggar, while the hand of God reaches down from the corner
portrait.credit: Saint Martin, Cretan-Venetian school, about 1500. Petit Palais, Paris. Paris Musées, CC0.
portrait.caption: An icon painted in Venetian Crete, about 1500. He cuts his cloak for the beggar, and the hand of God reaches down. Petit Palais, Paris. CC0.

typeNote: Confident here means steady and hard to rattle, never proud. His cloak also stands for The Giver, one of the test's seven roles.

west.text: In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**: his body moved, and his church at Tours dedicated.
**Catholic** memorial. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: **Russian Church**, on the old calendar. That is 25 October on today's calendar.

feasts.note: Why 11 November? He died on the 8th and was buried on the 11th, and the West keeps the day of his burial. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so 12 November falls on 25 November.

traits.title: patient with a hard man
traits.text: His own priest, Brictio, was abusive. Martin kept him on, and often said, “If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio?” Brictio became bishop after him, and is remembered as St Brice.

traits.title: always the same
traits.text: His disciple says no one ever saw him angry or excited, grieving or laughing. His face showed “a kind of heavenly happiness”.

traits.title: gave it all away
traits.text: He was given a gift of silver, and he gave it away. His monks were hungry and in rags. He told them, “Let the church both feed and clothe us, as long as we do not appear to have provided, in any way, for our own wants.”

traits.title: no flatterer
traits.text: At a banquet, he passed the emperor's cup to his own priest, “as thinking no one worthier to drink next to himself”.

said.lede: Almost everything we know comes from one friend. Sulpicius Severus wrote his *Life of St Martin* while Martin was still alive.

quotes.q: Never did a single hour or moment pass in which he was not either actually engaged in prayer; or, if it happened that he was occupied with something else, still he never let his mind loose from prayer.
…in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself.
quotes.who: Sulpicius Severus, on the emperor's court, where the other bishops gave way

quotes.q: For who ever suffered but Martin suffered along with him?

moments.title: The cloak
moments.text: One bitter winter, at the gate of Amiens, a man with no clothes begged, and everyone walked past him. Martin had already given away his other clothes. So he cut his soldier's cloak in two with his sword and gave the man half. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing that half. Christ said to the angels, “Martin, who is still but a catechumen, clothed Me with this robe.”

moments.title: Leaving the army
moments.text: Julian, then Caesar, was handing out a bonus to his men. Martin asked to leave the army instead. Called a coward, he offered to stand unarmed in front of the battle line the next day. The enemy asked for peace first.

moments.title: Hilary, and a monastery
moments.text: Free of the army, he went to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Hilary wanted to make him a deacon, but Martin kept saying he was unworthy. So Hilary made him an exorcist, a lowly office Martin would not refuse. After years of travel, he set up a monastery near Poitiers, at Ligugé. It may have been the first in Gaul.

cite.text: Life of St Martin, chapters 5 to 7

moments.title: Made bishop
moments.text: Tours wanted him as its bishop, but he would not leave his monastery. So a citizen threw himself at his knees and said his wife was ill. Martin came out, and crowds along the road led him into the city. A few bishops said he looked shabby and his hair was a mess. The people laughed at them and had their way.

moments.title: A hidden monastery
moments.text: As bishop he still lived as a monk. When the crowds of visitors grew too much, he built a hidden monastery about two miles outside the city. His wooden cell stood between a cliff and the Loire. About eighty disciples lived there, and they owned nothing.

moments.title: Before the emperor
moments.text: At the court of the emperor Maximus, the other bishops flattered him. Martin would not. He begged Maximus not to put the followers of the heretic Priscillian to death. He said being put out of the Church was punishment enough, and a ruler should not judge a church case. Once, to save men already sentenced, he took communion for a day with the bishops who had pressed for the killings. He grieved over it for the rest of his life, and never went to a synod again.

cite.text: Life, chapter 20; Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 50; Dialogue III, chapters 11 to 13

miracles.lede: Sulpicius tells dozens of wonders. He knew they would be doubted, and he made a promise at the start of the *Life*.

pledge.q: I implore those who are to read what follows to give full faith to the things narrated, and to believe that I have written nothing of which I had not certain knowledge and evidence.

items.title: The catechumen
items.text: A catechumen had joined Martin's monastery. He died of a fever while Martin was away, before he could be baptised. Martin sent everyone out, lay down on the body and prayed. Within about two hours the man began to move. He was baptised and lived for many years.
items.quote: they beheld the man alive whom they had formerly left dead
items.witness: The man told the story himself. He said he had stood before God's judgment, until two angels said he was the man Martin was praying for.

items.title: The slave
items.text: Passing the estate of Lupicinus, a man of high standing, Martin found a crowd wailing. One of the household's slaves had hanged himself. Martin went in alone, lay on the body and prayed. The dead man woke, took Martin's right hand and stood up. Then he walked with Martin to the porch, in front of everyone.
items.quote: with life beaming in his countenance, and with his drooping eyes fixed on Martin's face
items.witness: The whole crowd saw him walk out, says Sulpicius.

items.title: The only son
items.text: They passed a village where no one knew a single Christian, and a huge crowd of pagans came out to meet him. A mother held up her dead son and begged him. Martin took the body in his arms, knelt and prayed, and gave the child back to her alive. The crowd asked to become Christians on the spot, and he made them all catechumens there in the plain.
items.quote: We know that you are a friend of God: restore me my son, who is my only one.
items.witness: Gallus, his disciple, was there: “I myself am a witness to this latter occurrence”.

note.text: Martin used to tell Sulpicius that as a bishop he had less power to work wonders than he had before.

more.title: The falling pine
more.text: Martin had torn down a village's old temple, and he meant to cut down the sacred pine beside it. The pagans made him a deal: they would cut it down themselves if he stood where it fell. They bound him and set him where it would fall. As the tree came down, he raised his hand and made the sign of the cross. It swung round and fell the other way. Almost the whole crowd asked to become Christians that day.
more.quote: it swept round to the opposite side, to such a degree that it almost crushed the rustics

more.title: The leper at Paris
more.text: At the gate of Paris, with crowds around him, Martin kissed a leper and blessed him. The man was cleansed. The next day he came to church with healthy skin to give thanks.
more.quote: he gave a kiss to a leper, of miserable appearance, while all shuddered at seeing him do so

more.title: Paulinus's eye
more.text: Paulinus, later the famous bishop of Nola, had a thick skin growing over the pupil of one eye, and it hurt badly. Martin touched it with a paintbrush, and the pain went and the eye was healed.
more.quote: Martin touched his eye with a painter's brush

more.title: A globe of fire
more.text: On a great feast day, as Martin blessed the altar, a ball of fire rose from his head, trailing a long flame. The church was crowded, but only five people saw it: one consecrated virgin, one priest and three monks.
more.quote: we beheld a globe of fire dart from his head

doubt.title: Doubted from the start
doubt.text: Doubters came early. A friend told Sulpicius of one man who said he had “told many lies in that book of yours”. In the last *Dialogue*, Gallus says many doubted what he had told the day before. So from then on he names living witnesses, people a doubter could go and ask.

words.note: Martin wrote nothing that survives. These are his words as Sulpicius Severus recorded them, in Alexander Roberts's translation of 1894.

feature.q: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
feature.ctx: To Julian, then Caesar, when he asked to leave the army. In Latin, {la|Christi ego miles sum: pugnare mihi non licet.}

quotes.q: The Lord Jesus did not predict that He would come clothed in purple, and with a glittering crown upon His head. I will not believe that Christ has come, unless He appears with that appearance and form in which He suffered, and openly displaying the marks of His wounds upon the cross.
quotes.who: The devil came to him dressed as a king and claimed to be Christ. Sulpicius says he heard this from Martin himself.

quotes.q: See, she has fulfilled the precept of the Gospel: she had two coats, and one of them she has given to him who had none: thus, therefore, ye ought also to do.
quotes.who: On seeing a sheep that had just been shorn.

quotes.q: This is a picture of how the demons act: they lie in wait for the unwary and capture them before they know it: they devour their victims when taken, and they can never be satisfied with what they have devoured.
quotes.who: On his last journey, watching water-birds dive for fish.

quotes.q: The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do unto me.
quotes.who: To the devil, on the road past Milan. He is quoting Psalm 118.

myths.claim: He hid among geese to escape being made bishop, and their honking gave him away. That is why geese are eaten at Martinmas.
myths.truth: A later legend. Sulpicius tells a different story: a citizen pretended his wife was ill, to get Martin out of his monastery.

cite.text: Life of St Martin, chapter 9; New Liturgical Movement, 2022

myths.claim: He gave only half his cloak because the other half belonged to the army.
myths.truth: Sulpicius does not say this. He says Martin had nothing left but the cloak, “for he had already parted with the rest of his garments for similar purposes”.

myths.claim: When he woke, his cloak was whole again.
myths.truth: Not in Sulpicius, who says nothing of the cloak being restored. *Britannica* tells it as a legend.

cite.text: Life of St Martin, chapter 3; Britannica

myths.claim: He was riding a horse when he met the beggar.
myths.truth: Sulpicius never mentions a horse. The painters added it, as El Greco did.

myths.claim: He said it to the emperor Julian the Apostate.
myths.truth: Julian was then Caesar, a junior ruler, not yet emperor. Sulpicius writes “Julian Cæsar”.

cite.text: Life of St Martin, chapters 2 and 4

myths.claim: His sermons, or his Confession of Faith.
myths.truth: Nothing he wrote survives. The confession of faith once credited to him is not thought to be his.

stood.lede: Each line is Martin’s, as Sulpicius Severus recorded it.

death.big: He died of a fever in old age, at Candes in his own diocese, on 8 November 397.
paras: He had gone there to make peace among the local clergy. He knew his end was near. Once they were reconciled, his strength failed, and his disciples begged him not to leave them.
He died lying on sackcloth and ashes, praying, with his eyes on heaven. He would not let them put straw under him. He was buried at Tours three days later.
Sulpicius was not there. Two monks from Tours brought him the news.

later.title: A later story
later.text: Gregory of Tours, writing about 590, says the people of Poitiers and Tours fought over the body. At midnight the men of Tours passed it out of a window. They took it by boat down the Vienne and the Loire to Tours. Gregory ran Martin's shrine, so treat his extra stories as late.

cite.text: History of the Franks, Book 1, chapter 48

items.q: O Lord, if I am still necessary to Thy people, I do not shrink from toil: Thy will be done.

items.k: His last words, to the devil
items.q: Why do you stand here, thou bloody monster? Thou shalt find nothing in me, thou deadly one: Abraham's bosom is about to receive me.
items.ctx: “As he uttered these words, his spirit fled.”

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: He was honoured as a saint from the first. He was one of the first saints honoured who did not die as a martyr. His disciple saw it coming:

quotes.q: …although the character of our times could not ensure him the honor of martyrdom, yet he will not remain destitute of the glory of a martyr.
At Tours, in France, the birthday of blessed Martin, bishop and confessor, whose life was so renowned for miracles that he received the power to raise three persons from the dead.
quotes.who: The *Roman Martyrology*, 1916 edition, for 11 November. In its own words, a saint's “birthday” is “the day on which a Saint enters heaven”.

kin.name: Benedict of Nursia
kin.text: As a young man he ran from praise and lived three years alone in a cave. When his own monks tried to poison him, he faced them “with a mild countenance and quiet mind”. When a raging Goth shouted at him to get up, the Goth ended at his feet, and Benedict “rose not up from his reading”.

kin.name: John the Baptist
kin.text: He lived in the wilderness until the day he began to preach. Jesus asked the crowds if they had gone out to see “a reed swaying in the wind”. St Gregory says a reed bends to praise or blame, but “no variety of circumstance bent him from his uprightness”.
kin.cite: Luke 1:80; Matthew 11:7; St Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels

kin.name: Mary of Bethany
kin.text: When Jesus came to their home, her sister Martha was busy with all the preparations. Mary sat at His feet and listened. Jesus said she “has chosen the good portion”.
